expedient

ek-SPEE-dee-uhnt -- from Latin expedire, 'to free the feet,' from ex- ('out') + pes/ped- ('foot') -- literally to disentangle the feet and get moving. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Expedient is convenient and advantageous.

Building a temporary footbridge was the most expedient way to reconnect the two halves of the flooded village.

Example

A company facing a public complaint finds it more expedient to issue a quick refund than to investigate what actually went wrong.

Expedient describes exactly that kind of quick, practical fix -- convenient for solving today's problem, even if it skips a deeper solution.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

pragmatic: Pragmatic describes a whole way of thinking -- a pragmatic person weighs what actually works over theories and ideals, and the word is usually a compliment. Expedient judges one particular choice, often with a raised eyebrow: the expedient option is the quick, advantageous fix, even when a better, slower answer exists.

practical: Practical means sensible and workable -- a practical plan actually gets the job done with the tools at hand, and the word carries no criticism. Expedient adds a sharper edge: an expedient choice is made because it is quick and advantageous right now, sometimes at the cost of principle or thoroughness.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

impractical: not sensible or workable

idealistic: guided by principle rather than practical convenience

Where it sits · how much quick advantage drives the choice

convenient → expedient → opportunistic

convenient vs. expedient: Convenient is milder than expedient -- something convenient is simply easy or handy, while expedient specifically means chosen because it's the quickest practical fix for an immediate problem, sometimes overlooking a better long-term option.

opportunistic vs. expedient: Opportunistic goes a step beyond expedient -- an expedient choice at least aims to solve a real problem quickly, while an opportunistic one simply grabs whatever advantage the moment offers, with principle set aside altogether.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ex-: out (Latin)

root — -ped-: foot (Latin (pes, pedis))

suffix — -ient: doing or being; forms an adjective (variant of -ent) (Latin)

Put it together: Latin expedire meant 'to free the feet' -- ex- ('out') plus ped- ('foot') -- and the suffix -ient forms the adjective. An expedient choice untangles your feet and gets things moving quickly, whether or not it is the noblest path.

Use the root in a new word: impede: A single broken elevator can impede deliveries to the building's upper floors for an entire afternoon.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Expedient often carries a faint hint of criticism -- an expedient choice solves the immediate problem but may sacrifice principle or thoroughness to do it quickly, which is different from something simply 'practical.'
